The initial life stages of the long-armed burrowing brittlestar Amphiura filiformis are tightly coupled to the low water temperatures typical of its North Sea habitat. Following external fertilisation, the fertilised eggs develop rapidly, with the ophiopluteus larva hatching at approximately 1.5 days at 14 °C [T = 14 °C] and an age of 1.5 days . By day two, the embryos have transitioned into free-swimming ophiopluteus larvae, marking an age at birth of 2 days [ab = 2 days] under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C]. The total length of the newly hatched ophiopluteus, measured from representative images, is 0.0075 cm , which is identical to the total length at birth of 0.0075 cm [Lb = 0.0075 cm]. These tiny, planktonic larvae are initially endotrophic, subsisting on yolk reserves before commencing exogenous feeding on phytoplankton. The wet weight at birth, calculated from an assumed egg diameter of 0.1 mm, is an extraordinarily slight 0.0000005236 grams [Wwb = 0.0000005236 grams], reflecting the diminutive size of the broadcast eggs from which they emerge.

The planktonic larval phase of Amphiura filiformis culminates in a dramatic metamorphic event during which the bilateral ophiopluteus undergoes body plan reorganisation into a benthic juvenile. At a temperature of 14 °C [T = 14 °C], this metamorphic climax is reached after an average of 17 days , with the settlement length serving as a proxy for the total length at metamorphosis of 0.0325 cm . This value represents a substantial increase in body size from the hatching stage, driven by planktotrophic feeding during the larval phase. The timing of this larval-juvenile transition is critical for recruitment success, as competent larvae must locate suitable soft-bottom substrata for settlement. Upon completion of arm resorption and adult rudiment development, the newly metamorphosed juveniles begin their infaunal existence within the sediment. The entire process from egg to settled juvenile occurs rapidly, a life-history strategy that may enhance survival in a variable benthic environment where predation pressure on planktonic stages is high.

Juvenile growth and the progression toward sexual maturation in A. filiformis are protracted, with the onset of reproductive activity occurring after several years in the cold waters of the North Sea. The mean annual temperature of the habitat is approximately 6.8 °C [T = 6.8 °C], and under these conditions, first reproduction is documented to occur at 1,095 days after hatching [tR = 1,095 days after hatching]. This delayed age at first spawning contrasts with the rapid early development and reflects the substantial energetic investment required to build the reproductive biomass. The oral width at puberty, derived from an original disc diameter of 4 mm, is 0.138 cm [Lp = 0.138 cm]. This measurement of the oral frame provides a stable proxy for assessing the onset of gametogenesis in individual brittlestars, as disc diameter can be variable. The wet weight at puberty, calculated from disc diameter using established morphometric equations, reaches 4.7756 grams [Wwp = 4.7756 grams], indicating that individuals must acquire considerable somatic tissue before commencing gamete production.

Fully mature adults of A. filiformis achieve an ultimate oral width of 0.29 centimeters [Li = 0.29 centimeters], a measurement derived from populations outside the core study area as disc diameter is considered less stable. This maximum oral frame size corresponds to the max disc size reported in Swedish populations, providing a consistent upper limit for this morphological metric. The corresponding ultimate wet weight at this mature size is 5.8465 grams [Wwi = 5.8465 grams]. Reproductive output under optimal conditions is considerable, with individuals capable of producing 806.45 offspring per day [Ri = 806.45 offspring per day] during the spawning season when water temperatures average 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. This peak daily reproductive rate is sustained over the breeding period, with females releasing gametes into the water column in synchrony with other members of the population. The high fecundity is typical of broadcast-spawning echinoderms and compensates for the high mortality rates experienced by planktonic larvae.

The demographic structure of A. filiformis populations is shaped by its remarkable longevity, with individuals inhabiting a thermal environment of 6.8 °C [T = 6.8 °C] exhibiting a maximum lifespan of 9,125 days [am = 9,125 days]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 25 years, allows for multiple reproductive seasons and contributes to the species' role as a dominant member of the infaunal community in muddy sand habitats of the North Sea and adjacent waters. Field surveys and long-term studies, such as those by Ocklemann and Muus in 1978, have provided the foundation for these demographic parameters. The slow life-history pace is energetically supported by a feeding strategy that combines deposit and suspension feeding, allowing the brittlestar to exploit both sedimentary organic matter and suspended particulates. This trophic flexibility likely buffers the population against interannual variability in food supply. The ability to achieve exceptional ages also facilitates the accumulation of large body sizes and high reproductive output over the lifetime of each individual.
